input:
הייתי חייב לנצח בקרב הזה.
הסתתרתי מאחורי גזע עץ רחב וניסיתי לשמור על שקט מוחלט, ללא כישופים. בזבוז אנרגייה כדי להיטמע בסביבה זו טעות של טירונים. או של דרומיים.
הבטתי בגבו של היריב שלי בזמן שבחן את עץ האלון שלפניו. הוא לא זז. כנראה חיכה, כמוני, לתנועה לא נכונה, להזדמנות לתקוף.
גלי אנרגייה עוצמתיים זרמו ממנו לכל כיוון כשהחליט סוף־סוף לפעול. שוט אנרגייה כחול ובוהק התגבש בידו והוא תקף את העץ בשתי הצלפות חלקות. כשמיקמתי את הבובה מאחורי העץ, ידעתי שהוא ימצא אותה וינסה לתקוף אותה.
לא ציפיתי שיצליח לחתוך את הגזע ולהפיל את העץ כולו על האדמה.
אבל זה לא משנה. הוא היה מרוכז בעץ ואני קיבלתי את ההזדמנות שלי לתקוף.
"אני לא בטוח שאתה מבין מה זה אומר להסתתר," הוא גיחך בקול מתנשא לכיוון הבובה.
חייכתי. לא יכולתי לעצור את עצמי. "ואני לא בטוח שאתה מבין מה זה אומר לחשוב."
הוא הסתובב אליי בבת אחת, אבל כבר היה מאוחר מדי. האנרגייה שלי געשה החוצה בגלים, מתחברת לאנרגייה של אחד העצים עד שיכולתי לפקוד עליו כרצוני. ענפיו של העץ התארכו ונמתחו, עד שהתלפפו מסביב ליריב שלי.
"הפסדת," ציינתי. ניסיתי להקרין ביטחון, אבל הביטחון הזה החל להתערער כשהבנתי שהוא מחייך.
"לא," שמעתי את החיוך בקולו, "אתה הפסדת ברגע שבחרת לנסות לתקוף אותי עם עצים. האמת? ציפיתי ממך ליותר."
הענפים שנכרכו סביבו החלו להתרופף וגלי האנרגייה שלי נהדפו, כאילו העץ דוחה אותם במטרה לקלוט את גלי האנרגייה של היריב שלי. למשך כמה שניות עוד החזקתי בעץ תחת שליטתי, אבל בו־זמנית יכולתי לראות בעיני רוחי את כוחותיו של המכשף השני – עוצמתיים ובוהקים, דוחפים את האנרגייה שלי החוצה. כמה שניות אחר כך איבדתי אחיזה בעץ. ארבעה ענפים נשלחו לכיווני במהירות מסחררת, נכרכו סביב ידיי ורגליי ולפני שהספקתי להגיב, מצאתי את עצמי מונף באוויר.
"תיכנע."
חשקתי את שיניי וניסיתי להיאבק בענפים. איזה אידיוט אני.
הזוהר בעיניים שלו התחזק ומצאתי את עצמי תלוי במהופך, ראשי קרוב בצורה מרגיזה לקרקע.
"תיכנע," הוא חזר.
נשכתי את שפתיי בתסכול והתאמצתי לבטא את המילה, "נכנע."
הענפים הרפו ונפלתי על האדמה.
"2:1," גיל ציין בחיוך.
"רק כי בפעם הראשונה לא ידעתי שזו תחרות." התרוממתי וניקיתי את העפר והעלים הלחים שנדבקו לבגדיי.
שנאתי להפסיד לגיל. אימונים איתו בהחלט הוציאו את הצד התחרותי שבי. ידעתי שהוא חזק יותר, אבל אני הייתי חכם יותר ומיומן יותר – הוא לא היה אמור לנצח אותי בכזו בקלות.
notes: HEBREW - real-world passage from src/docs/test-text.txt. Consistent first-person past-tense battle scene with dialogue; a false-positive trap (local qwen3.5:4b wrongly flagged a dialogue line as register and a within-sentence tense nitpick mislabeled pov). All evaluated cloud models returned []. Validated by user 2026-06-17.

Daniel pushed open the cafe door and let the warmth fold around him. He had walked the long way again, the way that passed her old street, and he told himself it meant nothing. He found a table by the window and sat with his coat still on.

He ordered black coffee and turned the cup in his hands without drinking it. The radio behind the counter was playing something he half remembered. He watched the door and pretended he wasn't watching it.

When Mara finally came in, the cold air came with her. Daniel lifted his hand, then lowered it, unsure whether she had seen him. He rehearsed the first sentence in his head and hated every version of it.

Mara saw him at once and felt her stomach tighten. She had hoped he would not come, and now that he had, she did not know where to put her hands. She wondered if he could tell how little she had slept, and she decided that she would not be the first to apologize.

She crossed the room slowly, counting her own steps, holding the strap of her bag like a rope. Whatever he had come to say, she promised herself she would listen and give nothing away.
notes: English planted POV head-hop (the Daniel/Mara passage from the prior manual test). The chapter is firmly in Daniel's close third-person POV for the first three paragraphs (his walk, his rehearsed sentence, what he 'told himself'). The fourth paragraph head-hops into Mara's interiority ('felt her stomach tighten', 'she wondered', 'she decided') — a viewpoint Daniel cannot access. Only POV is planted; tense (past) and register (literary) are stable. Embedded in a longer self-contained chapter so a conservative model is more likely to miss it (gemma4:12b missed the shorter planted-pov-en in the pre-expansion baseline). Validated by author.

input:
דניאל דחף את דלת בית הקפה ונתן לחום לעטוף אותו. שוב הלך בדרך הארוכה, זו שעוברת ליד הרחוב הישן שלה, ואמר לעצמו שזה לא אומר כלום. הוא מצא שולחן ליד החלון והתיישב בלי להוריד את המעיל.

הוא הזמין קפה שחור וסובב את הספל בין ידיו בלי לשתות. הרדיו מאחורי הדלפק ניגן משהו שזכר במעורפל. הוא הביט בדלת והעמיד פנים שאינו מביט בה.

כשמרה סוף-סוף נכנסה, האוויר הקר נכנס איתה. דניאל הרים את ידו, ואז הוריד אותה, לא בטוח אם ראתה אותו. הוא חזר בראשו על המשפט הראשון ושנא כל גרסה שלו.

מרה ראתה אותו מיד והרגישה את הבטן שלה מתכווצת. היא קיוותה שלא יבוא, ועכשיו, כשבא, לא ידעה איפה להניח את הידיים. היא תהתה אם הוא מבחין כמה מעט ישנה, והחליטה בלבה שלא תהיה הראשונה להתנצל.

היא חצתה את החדר לאט, סופרת את צעדיה, אוחזת ברצועת התיק כמו בחבל. מה שלא בא לומר, הבטיחה לעצמה שתקשיב ולא תיתן לו דבר.
notes: HEBREW DRAFT — REQUIRES NATIVE SPEAKER VALIDATION. Hebrew mirror of planted-pov-headhop-en (the Daniel/Mara head-hop). First three paragraphs are close third-person on Daniel ('אמר לעצמו', 'חזר בראשו'). The fourth paragraph head-hops into Mara's interiority ('הרגישה את הבטן שלה מתכווצת', 'היא תהתה', 'החליטה בלבה') — inaccessible to Daniel's viewpoint. Only POV is planted; tense (past) and register (literary) stable. Native reviewer: confirm the head-hop reads as an unambiguous POV violation and that the prose is natural literary Hebrew.

input:
The harvest had ended early that year, and the village settled into the slow weeks before the cold. Old Tomas mended his nets by the door while the children chased the last of the geese across the yard. Everyone agreed it had been a kind autumn.

In the evenings the families gathered at the long house and shared what little news the road had carried. They spoke of the market town, of the price of salt, of a stranger who had passed through and asked too many questions. No one thought much of it at the time.

Tomas walks down to the water before dawn. He checks each net in turn and finds the third one torn. He kneels on the cold stones and works the knots loose, and he does not hear the footsteps behind him until they are very close.

By the time the others woke, Tomas was gone, and only the mended nets remained, folded neatly where he always left them.
notes: English planted tense slip (the past->present slip from the prior manual test). The chapter is past tense throughout ('had ended', 'mended', 'gathered', 'woke', 'was gone') except the third paragraph, which slips into present ('walks', 'checks', 'finds', 'kneels', 'does not hear'). The surrounding past-tense narration resumes in the final paragraph, making the slip a clear internal inconsistency rather than an intentional style. Only tense is planted; POV (third-person) and register (literary) are stable. Embedded in a longer chapter so the model must localize the slipped paragraph. Validated by author.

input:
הקציר הסתיים מוקדם באותה שנה, והכפר שקע בשבועות האיטיים שלפני הקור. תומס הזקן תיקן את הרשתות ליד הפתח, והילדים רדפו אחרי האווזים האחרונים בחצר. כולם הסכימו שזה היה סתיו רחום.

בערבים התאספו המשפחות בבית הארוך וחלקו את מעט החדשות שהדרך הביאה. הם דיברו על העיר, על מחיר המלח, על זר שעבר ושאל יותר מדי שאלות. איש לא חשב על כך הרבה באותו זמן.

תומס יורד אל המים לפני עלות השחר. הוא בודק כל רשת בתורה ומגלה שהשלישית קרועה. הוא כורע על האבנים הקרות ומשחרר את הקשרים, ואינו שומע את הצעדים מאחוריו עד שהם קרובים מאוד.

כשהאחרים התעוררו, תומס כבר איננו, ורק הרשתות המתוקנות נשארו, מקופלות בקפידה במקום שבו תמיד הניח אותן.
notes: HEBREW DRAFT — REQUIRES NATIVE SPEAKER VALIDATION. Hebrew mirror of planted-tense-slip-en. Past tense throughout ('הסתיים', 'תיקן', 'התאספו', 'התעוררו') except the third paragraph, which slips to present ('יורד', 'בודק', 'מגלה', 'כורע', 'אינו שומע'). Past-tense narration resumes in the final paragraph. Only tense is planted; POV (third-person) and register stable. Native reviewer: confirm the third paragraph reads unambiguously as a present-tense slip inside a past-tense narrative (Hebrew present-tense participles vs past-tense verbs) and that no other reading makes it intentional.

Rain had been falling since noon, and the lighthouse keeper climbed the iron stairs with a lamp in one hand. The steps were slick and the wind found every gap in the old walls. He had made this climb ten thousand times, and his knees remembered each one.

At the top he trimmed the wick and watched the beam swing out over the black water. A ship was somewhere out there, beating against the weather, and he wished it home the way he wished every ship home, quietly, without expecting an answer.

The operational parameters of the facility necessitate continuous illumination during periods of reduced visibility. Maintenance personnel are required to conduct hourly inspections of the apparatus and to document any deviation from the prescribed luminous output in the designated logbook.

He set the lamp down and pressed his forehead to the cold glass. Out in the dark, far off, a single light answered his, and he let out a breath he had not known he was holding.
notes: English planted register drift WITHIN the narration. Paragraphs 1, 2, and 4 are warm literary prose (the keeper's interior, sensory detail). Paragraph 3 abruptly shifts to dry bureaucratic/technical register ('operational parameters', 'necessitate continuous illumination', 'maintenance personnel are required', 'designated logbook') before the literary voice resumes. This is a narration-internal register shift (no dialogue involved), so it does NOT fall under the dialogue-vs-narration exemption. Only register is planted; tense (past) and POV (third-person) are stable. Validated by author.

input:
הגשם ירד מאז הצהריים, ושומר המגדלור טיפס במדרגות הברזל ובידו האחת מנורה. המדרגות היו חלקלקות והרוח מצאה כל סדק בקירות הישנים. הוא עשה את הטיפוס הזה אלפי פעמים, וברכיו זכרו כל אחת מהן.

במעלה גזר את הפתיל והביט באלומה נשלחת אל המים השחורים. אי-שם בחוץ הייתה ספינה, נאבקת במזג האוויר, והוא איחל לה שתשוב הביתה כפי שאיחל לכל ספינה, בשקט, בלי לצפות לתשובה.

Elias reached the top of the levee before the light did, and stood there letting his breath settle. The river was low for March. He had counted on that, the way he counted on most things, which was to say not at all and completely.

He walked the crest as far as the pumping station and back, checking the sandbags he had stacked in October. Two had split. He would have to tell someone, and telling someone meant the parish office, and the parish office meant Ruth.

The office opened at eight. He waited on the step until the lock turned, and then he went in and put his hat on the counter and waited some more while she finished a column of figures.

Ruth did not look up. Eight sandbags in October and he wanted a medal for it. The whole parish ran on men who did half a job and came in expecting to be thanked, and there was a form for that, and the form took twenty minutes, and there were four hundred parcels to reconcile before noon. Let him stand.

Elias cleared his throat. He said the river was low but the bags on the north crest had gone, and he said it twice, because the second time it sounded less like an apology.

The orchard came down to the road in rows so old the trees had forgotten how to stand straight, and in the last week of September the air under them went thick and sweet and faintly alcoholic. Miriam walked the rows at dusk with a basket she did not intend to fill. It was enough to be among them, to hear the small collapse of fruit in the grass.

Her grandmother had planted the first forty and had died believing that a tree remembers the hand that prunes it. Miriam had never been able to decide whether this was superstition or simply an unusually patient way of describing habit.

So anyway the harvest was a mess this year. Nobody showed up on the Tuesday, which was pretty much what she expected, and the pickers who did show up wanted cash and wanted it up front. She told them fine, whatever, just get the north end done before it rains. It rained.

By the first frost the fruit that remained had gone soft and brown and the wasps had come for it, and the rows at dusk smelled of cider and of something older than cider. Miriam walked them anyway, basket empty, listening.

She did not prune that winter. In the spring the trees came back crooked and generous, as they always had, and she chose to believe her grandmother had been right about the hand.

That case drops bureaucratic boilerplate ('operational parameters', 'designated logbook') into literary prose - a lexical flag any model can match on. It is narration, NOT dialogue, so the prompt's dialogue-vs-narration exemption does not apply. The literary voice resumes in paragraphs 4-5 so the shift cannot be read as the piece simply changing style for good. Only register is planted; tense (past) and POV (Miriam) are stable. Validated by author.

The snow started before they finished loading and did not stop for two days. Anna's father drove as far as the mill road and then admitted the truck would not take the grade, and they carried the last of it up on their backs, three trips each, the boxes going soft in the wet.

The house had stood empty since the spring. Someone had taken the stove and left the pipe, and there were mouse tracks across the counter in a fine grey dust that Anna wiped away with her sleeve before her mother could see it.

They slept in coats the first night. In the morning her father went down to the village for kindling and came back with kindling and a rumour, and the rumour was that the mill would reopen in April, and her mother said nothing at all to that, which was how Anna knew what her mother thought of it.

She stands at the window while they argue. The glass is cold enough to hurt and the field beyond it holds the last light longer than the sky does. Somewhere below, a dog is barking at nothing.

Her father won the argument by not continuing it. He went out to the woodpile and stayed there until the light was gone, and when he came back in he had split more than they could burn in a week, and nobody said anything about April again.

By February the snow had packed hard enough to walk on and Anna had stopped counting the days until the mill.

The bus came at ten past and Dov got on with everybody else and found a seat near the back where the heater worked. He had made this trip eleven times and he no longer looked out the window.

At the second stop a woman got on carrying a cage with nothing in it. She sat across the aisle. She set the cage on her knees and did not take her hands off it and did not speak to anyone for the whole hour.

The road beyond the depot ran between fields that had been ploughed since before the memory of men, and the dust of them lay upon every traveller alike, and it was said in that country that the earth keeps a fuller account of us than we keep of it.

Dov got off at the depot and stood a moment in the diesel smell, working out which way was north. The woman with the cage got off behind him and went the other way, and he did not think of her again until much later.

The letter came on a Thursday and Tom put it on the shelf behind the radio without opening it. He knew the handwriting. He had known it for forty years, and there was no version of the afternoon that would be improved by knowing more.

He had met her in the summer before the flood, when the town still had two garages and a picture house, and he had walked her home along the culvert road because that was what you did then. They had argued about nothing for a year and about something for a month, and then she had gone to her sister's in the city and had not written.

On Thursdays he always cleaned the yard. He would start at the gate and work in, and by four there would be a barrow of leaves and a clear path to the shed, and he would stand and look at it longer than a clear path deserved.

He cleaned the yard. He made his tea. At nine he took the letter down and read it standing up, and then he put it back on the shelf behind the radio, and he went to bed at the usual time.

Yosef climbed to the roof because the flat below was too warm to think in, and because the roof was the only place in the building where nobody asked him anything. He took the folding chair from behind the water tank and set it facing west, out of habit, though there was nothing to see that way but the backs of other buildings.

The girl from the fourth floor was already there. Her shoes were off and her feet were up on the parapet and her phone lay face down beside her. She did not look up when he came out, and she did not move when he dragged the chair across the tar, and after a while she picked up the phone and turned it over and turned it back.

He considered saying something and did not. He had been rehearsing a sentence for his mother for three days and it kept coming out wrong, and he suspected that speaking to anyone at all would use up the version of the sentence he currently had.

The girl stood, put her shoes on, and went down. Yosef stayed until the light went orange and then grey, and then he folded the chair and put it back behind the tank, and the sentence was no better than it had been.

The office smelled of toner and old coffee. Rina sat down and put the folder on her knees because there was nowhere else to put it.

"It is not, strictly speaking, a matter of entitlement," the clerk said. "The provision to which you refer confers a discretionary benefit upon persons in circumstances materially similar to your own, which is to say that the department may act and is under no obligation to do so."

Rina looked at the folder. Then she looked at him.

"So no," she said.

"I would not put it that way," he said. "I would say that the department retains a measure of latitude, and that the exercise of that latitude is informed by considerations which are not, in the ordinary course, disclosed to applicants."

She stood up. The chair squeaked. Outside, somebody was arguing with the lift.
